title: Korean Air 801

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Controlled Flight Into Terrain, Korean Air Flight 801, Boeing 747-300, HL7468, Nimitz Hill, Guam, August 6, 1997

location.name: Nimitz Hill, about 3 nm southwest of Guam International Airport

summary: Flying a night non-precision localizer approach to runway 6L at Guam in rain showers, with the glideslope out of service, the fatigued captain descended below the step-down altitudes as if on a glideslope while the first officer and flight engineer failed to challenge him effectively. The 747 struck Nimitz Hill about 3 nm short of the runway near the Nimitz VOR. The FAA's minimum safe altitude warning system, which could have alerted the controller, had been inhibited. 228 of the 254 on board died.
probable_cause: The captain's failure to adequately brief and execute the nonprecision approach and the first officer's and flight engineer's failure to effectively monitor and cross-check the captain's execution of the approach. Contributing to these failures were the captain's fatigue and Korean Air's inadequate flight crew training. Contributing to the accident was the Federal Aviation Administration's intentional inhibition of the minimum safe altitude warning system at Guam and the agency's failure to adequately manage the system.

factors.evidence: The captain did not adequately brief the localizer-only approach and descended below the published step-down altitudes before reaching the fixes.
The aircraft descended through the 2,000 ft and 1,440 ft step-down altitudes and through the 560 ft MDA without the runway in sight.
The captain remarked during the flight that he was really sleepy; the NTSB found his fatigue degraded his performance.
The first officer and flight engineer failed to monitor and cross-check the captain's execution of the approach.
Concerns about the approach were voiced indirectly and the call for a missed approach came too late to prevent impact.
The captain apparently believed the glideslope was usable and lost awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the step-down fixes.
The NTSB cited Korean Air's inadequate flight crew training in non-precision approaches and CRM.
The FAA had intentionally inhibited the Guam MSAW system to eliminate nuisance alerts, so the controller received no warning of the descent.
The NTSB found the FAA failed to adequately manage the MSAW system at Guam.
Rain showers on the approach path intermittently obscured the runway.
The approach was flown at about 01:40 local time in darkness.
GPWS altitude and sink rate callouts were heard but the go-around was not initiated until seconds before impact.
The aircraft struck Nimitz Hill at about 660 ft elevation near the Nimitz VOR, about 3 nm from the runway.
The wreckage burned after impact; fire and delayed rescue contributed to the death toll.

events.text: During the descent the captain remarks that he is really sleepy.
Captain briefs the approach to runway 6L, referring to the ILS although the glideslope is out of service per NOTAM; the briefing does not cover the step-down fixes of the localizer approach.
Guam CERAP clears the flight for the ILS runway 6L approach, noting the glideslope is unusable, and hands the flight to Agana tower.
Crew discuss whether the glideslope is working after seeing intermittent indications; the captain appears to believe a glideslope is available.
Aircraft enters rain showers on final; the runway lights are intermittently visible.
Aircraft descends below 2,000 ft before reaching the Nimitz VOR step-down fix.
Aircraft continues descent below the 1,440 ft step-down altitude and below the 560 ft MDA; the inhibited MSAW gives the controller no alert.
GPWS radio altitude callout 'one thousand' sounds.
Flight engineer and first officer note that the runway is not in sight; GPWS 'minimums' and 'sink rate' callouts follow.
First officer calls for a missed approach.
Captain calls go around and begins to advance the throttles.
Aircraft strikes trees and terrain on Nimitz Hill near the Nimitz VOR, about 3 nm southwest of the runway 6L threshold, and breaks up; fire follows.
Rescue efforts are delayed by the terrain, a broken pipeline and coordination problems; 26 people survive.

recommendations.text: Review and correct the inhibition of MSAW systems at all ATC facilities and establish procedures to ensure MSAW is not inappropriately inhibited.
recommendations.outcome: The FAA restored full MSAW coverage at Guam and reviewed MSAW configurations nationwide.

recommendations.text: Require air carriers to provide flight crews with training and procedures for non-precision approaches, including constant-angle descent techniques.
recommendations.outcome: Constant descent final approach techniques were widely adopted for non-precision approaches.

recommendations.text: Require terrain awareness and warning systems (enhanced GPWS) on transport category aircraft.
recommendations.outcome: FAA required TAWS on turbine aircraft with six or more passenger seats by 2005.

recommendations.text: Improve Korean Air's flight crew training, CRM and fatigue management and strengthen Korean oversight of the airline.
recommendations.outcome: Korean Air overhauled its training and safety programs following this and subsequent accidents.

safety_changes: FAA restored MSAW coverage at Guam and audited MSAW inhibition at other facilities.
Korean Air restructured its flight operations, training and CRM programs after a series of accidents.
Wider adoption of constant descent angle non-precision approaches and of terrain awareness warning systems.

notes: t0 is the impact time 01:42:26 local; the GPWS 'one thousand' callout and first officer's missed approach call times are recalled from the report to within a few seconds; earlier event times are approximate.
Fatalities: the NTSB report gives 228 of 254 occupants; some sources count later deaths differently.
Korean accredited representative agency code 'KCAB' is a shorthand for the Korean Civil Aviation Bureau of the time.
Recommendation numbers not recalled and are left null.
